readerTitle: How to get help from people who don't report to you
caseNote: 가상 사례 (마케팅 에이전시, 호텔 레스토랑) + 실제 연구 프레임워크 (Cohen & Bradford의 '통화' 교환 모델). 실제 기업 사례 대신 정확성을 위해 일상 장면 형식으로 변경
insight: 권한이 없을 때의 영향력은 설득하는 말재주가 아니라, 상대가 중요하게 여기는 것을 알아내고 그것과 내 요청을 교환하는 일이다.
misconception: 권한이 없으면 더 강하게 설득하거나 상사를 통해 밀어붙이는 수밖에 없다.

sources.text: Cohen, A. R., & Bradford, D. L. Influence Without Authority. Wiley (1st ed. 1990; later editions 2005, 2017).
에이전시와 레스토랑 장면은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Cohen & Bradford 책의 초판·개정판 연도(1990, 2005, 2017)를 게시 전에 출판사 자료로 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도 없이 '두 경영학 교수'로만 적었습니다.
5번 카드의 '통화' 목록(업무 도움, 정보, 인정, 시간 절약, 경청 등)은 책의 분류를 쉬운 말로 요약한 것입니다. 책의 원래 범주명과 표현을 그대로 옮긴 것이 아니므로, 직접 인용처럼 보이지 않는지 확인하세요.
레슨에 수치는 없습니다. 가상 장면의 결과(테오가 작업 순서를 바꿈 등)는 설명용입니다.

cards.title: How to get help from people who don't report to you
body: Maya runs client accounts at a marketing agency. Her biggest client needs new ad designs by Friday.
The designers sit ten meters away. None of them report to her. Their boss, Theo, already has a full week.

image.label: A woman at one desk looking across the office at a busy design team
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 한쪽 책상에 앉은 여성(마야)이 노트북을 들고, 반대편에서 모니터에 파묻혀 바쁘게 일하는 디자인팀을 바라봄. 두 공간 사이에 보이지 않는 선처럼 바닥 색이 다름. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: You need Theo's team. You can't order them.
body: Theo is polite but stretched. If you were Maya, what would you do first?

options.text: Ask the agency director to tell Theo to prioritize it
options.feedback: It may work once. But Theo learns that you go over his head, and next time he'll give you exactly the minimum.

options.text: Explain clearly how big this client is for the agency
options.feedback: It's honest and sometimes enough. But it's still your reason, not his, and every account lead says their client matters most.

options.text: Ask Theo what's making his week hard, then look for something you can fix
options.feedback: It costs a conversation and maybe some effort on your side. In return, you find a reason for him to say yes.

cards.title: The answer was something Maya could fix.
body: Theo's problem wasn't the deadline. It was revisions. Maya's clients sent vague briefs, then four rounds of scattered feedback from different people.
Maya offered a deal: she would get a signed-off brief before work started and collect all client comments into one round. Theo moved her job up.
The next quarter, when a slot opened, Theo called Maya first.

cards.title: Influence without authority
body: **Influence without authority** means getting people to act when you can't tell them to. You do it by giving them something they value in return.

Two business professors, Allan Cohen and David Bradford, called these things **currencies**. Your request costs the other person something. The trade works when you pay in a currency they care about, not the one you assume they want.

image.label: Two people exchanging different-shaped tokens across a table
image.brief: 두 사람이 테이블을 사이에 두고 서로 다른 모양의 토큰을 주고받는 장면. 한쪽 토큰에는 'Your request', 다른 쪽에는 'What they value' 라벨. 동전처럼 보이되 실제 화폐 기호는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Learn their world before you ask.
body: People value different things. Common currencies include:
list: **Help with the work:** fewer revisions, cleaner inputs, an extra pair of hands
**Information:** early news, useful data, context they lack
**Recognition:** credit in front of their boss or team
**Time back:** taking a task off their plate
**Being heard:** a real say in how something is done
cards.callout: Ask what they're judged on and what wastes their time. The currency is usually there.
cards.softwareNote: A product manager can't order engineers around. Good ones trade in currencies engineers value: clear specs, fewer last-minute changes, and time set aside to fix old code.

cards.title: Peers, bosses, suppliers, partners.
body: The same trade works sideways with peers, upward with your boss, and outward with suppliers and partners. A supplier rushes your order because you pay on time and send clear forecasts.
It also works best when you've built the relationship before you need it. A favor offered in a quiet week is worth more than a deal struck in a panic.

cards.title: A trade only works if it's real.
body: If you promise one feedback round and deliver four, you've spent trust you can't easily earn back. Keep every side of the deal.
Don't turn every request into a negotiation either. Constant bargaining feels transactional.
And some things need authority. If a safety or legal issue is at stake and the trade fails, escalate openly and say why.

cards.title: Now it's a hotel restaurant.
body: You manage the dining room. The head chef doesn't report to you. Allergy orders often come back wrong, and guests complain to your servers.
You want the kitchen to handle allergy tickets more carefully. What's your best move?

options.text: Ask the hotel manager to make it a kitchen rule
options.feedback: A rule may be justified, since allergies are a safety issue. But a forced rule without the chef's buy-in is often followed loosely.

options.text: Ask the chef what makes allergy tickets hard, and let him design the format servers use
options.feedback: He gets clearer tickets and fewer remakes during service. You get fewer mistakes. If it still fails, you can escalate with a clear conscience.

options.text: Post the guest complaints in the kitchen so the team sees the problem
options.feedback: It shows the problem, but it feels like blame. The kitchen may defend itself instead of changing.

cards.title: Pay in their currency, not yours.
body: When you can't order someone to help, find out what they value and offer it in return. Then keep your side of the deal.
**Try it today:** pick one person whose help you need but can't command. Write down what they're judged on and one thing you could take off their plate.
